system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2175-01-03 17:40:00 to 2175-01-04 15:52:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

COMPARISON:  Knee radiographs available from ___.

TWO VIEWS OF THE RIGHT KNEE:  There is diffuse osteopenia, limiting evaluation
of the fine cortical detail.  No acute fracture or dislocation is detected. 
There is no sclerotic or lytic lesion seen.  No joint effusion is present. 
Extensive vascular calcifications are seen.  There is no embedded radiopaque
foreign body.

3 VIEWS RIGHT TIBIA & FIBULA:  Diffuse osteopenia is present, limiting the
evaluation of the finer cortical detail.  There is no acute fracture or
dislocation seen.  No sclerotic or lytic lesions are detected.  Extensive
vascular calcifications are re-demonstrated.

IMPRESSION: 1)  Diffuse osteopenia, limiting evaluation of the fine cortical
detail. 2) No acute fracture or dislocation seen.

INDICATION:  Pain.

No comparison studies available.

THREE VIEWS OF THE LEFT SHOULDER:  There is no acute fracture or dislocation. 
Evaluation of the joint space is limited due to body habitus.  An old
deformity of the proximal left humerus is present, and may reflect a prior
traumatic event.  There is no sclerotic or lytic lesion detected.  There is no
embedded radiopaque foreign body.  Included views of the left upper chest are
unremarkable.

IMPRESSION:
1.  No acute fracture or dislocation.
2.  No soft tissue abnormalities such as calcific tendinitis are seen,
although the evaluation is limited due to body habitus.  Please note that MRI
is more sensitive for ligamentous/tendinous injury if no contraindication.

FINDINGS:  Grayscale, color and Doppler images were obtained of the right
common femoral, superficial femoral, popliteal and tibial veins.  There is
normal flow, compression and augmentation seen in all of the vessels.

IMPRESSION:  No evidence of deep vein thrombosis in the right leg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you’ve been having pain in your right leg and some fevers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. It started a few days ago. I went to another clinic and they gave me pills, but the fever came back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You also had your dialysis today before coming in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, right before I came here. I’ve been feeling weak and feverish since then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your leg and it looks red and warm—signs of cellulitis, which is a skin infection. We’ve started you on IV vancomycin to treat it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that strong enough? I was on antibiotics before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, this is stronger and given through the IV. We’re using it because the infection didn’t clear with the oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve also had some shoulder pain. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an X-ray of your shoulder and there’s no fracture or dislocation. It may be joint pain from gout or arthritis, but it’s not the main issue right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had gout before. I stopped taking prednisone because it made my arms weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but we recommend you take it as prescribed when needed. For now, we’re keeping you on your regular allopurinol and colchicine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your ultrasound from this morning shows no blood clot in your leg, which is great news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, good. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, your vancomycin level came back high enough to fight the infection. You’ll get the next dose during your next dialysis session.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll get the antibiotic at dialysis for a while?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’ll get IV vancomycin during dialysis for 10 days total. Keep your leg elevated and clean. The redness is already improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re discharging you home today. Continue all your regular medications, especially prednisone if your doctor prescribes it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if my leg starts hurting more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your primary doctor or come back to the ER if you get a fever, increased redness, or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay on top of your dialysis and meds. We’ll see you in follow-up soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis was admitted with right leg cellulitis and fever after incomplete response to oral antibiotics. He was started on IV vancomycin, which was adjusted based on trough levels. Imaging ruled out DVT and fractures. His infection improved during the short hospital stay, and he was discharged home with a plan to complete a 10-day course of IV vancomycin during dialysis sessions. He was advised to continue all home medications, including those for gout, coronary artery disease, and hypertension, and to follow up with his primary care provider regarding medication adherence.
